abstract
Pironetin is a unique a-tubulin inhibitor and has been of utmost interest in the synthetic community.
Based on the enabling method to access various stereotriads and stereotetrads, we devised a new total
synthesis of pironetin, a total 13 steps from commercially available ( S)-Roche ester, representing one of
the shortest synthetic routes reported to date. The facile fragmentation induced by the deprotonation of
the pyrone ring at C4 led us to reorient the installation of the remote enone moiety prior to the lactone
ring formation. Moreover, the undesired Michael addition of a phosphate reagent to the acrylate guided
us to introduce a sterically demanding cinnamate motif that was also found to facilitate the selective
removal of the TBDPS group. The evolution of the synthetic route underlines that the experimental
execution of the reactivity of various functional groups is instrumental to devise a successful synthesis.

1. Introduction
Anticancer agents targeting microtubules are among the most
powerful drugs used for chemotherapy cancer treatments [ 1]. All
such therapeutics in current clinical use were designed to bind b-
tubulin, a subunit that forms an a/b-heterodimer that is assembled
into a ﬁlamentous tube-shape structure and plays a pivotal role in
cell division during various stages of mitosis [ 2]. However, during
chemotherapy, the overexpression of b-tubulin isoforms that may
bind less ef ﬁciently to anticancer drugs induces severe drug-
resistance [ 3]. While the quest of more ef ﬁcient b-tubulin in-
hibitors is ongoing, an alternative approach for drug development
is to evaluate new leads that selectively interact with a-tubulin.
Pironetin is the only natural product currently known to bind to a-
tubulin [ 4]. The Chen and Steinmetz groups independently char-
acterized the a-tubulin-pironetin complex and revealed that pir-
onetin covalently binds to Cys-316 of a-tubulin via a Michael
addition ( Fig. 1 )[ 5,6]. The crystal structures further dictate that
pironetin perturbs the T7 loop and helix H8 of a-tubulin that are
crucial for establishing longitudinal tubulin contacts in microtu-
bules [ 6]. This structural information provides a solid molecular
basis for understanding the mechanism of the inhibition of the
formation of microtubules. Thus, pironetin is considered to be a
promising lead compound for the inspiration to develop a new
generation of analogues with desirable properties.
Pironetin features a stereotetrad polypropionate chain and a
4,5-disubstituted pyrone motif and was independently isolated
from the fermentation broths of Streptomyces species by two
research groups [ 7e9]. In addition to its potential use as a potent
inhibitor of the cell cycle progression at the M-phase (IC50 5e25 ng/
mL) [10], its potency as a plant growth regulator may be bene ﬁcial
for producing dwarf plants [ 8b]. Pironetin also exhibits potent
immunosuppressive activity on the responses of T and B lympho-
cytes to mitogens [ 9]. Due to its intriguing bioactivities and rela-
tively low molecular weight compared to the other known tubulin
regulators, pironetin has been of utmost interest for the synthetic
community. Since the ﬁrst total synthesis and structural con ﬁr-
mation of pironetin (PA-48153C) by Kawada and coworkers in 1995
[11], twelve synthetic routes and several structural derivatizations
of pironetin have been reported [ 12e14]. The conventional syn-
thetic strategies largely relied on the classical enantioselective aldol
reactions and allylations to construct the stereotetrad fragment
(C7eC10). Despite numerous synthetic efforts toward such struc-
turally signi ﬁcant polypropionates in the past decades [ 14], a

further application for accessing various analogues remain insuf-
ﬁcient. During our effort to develop a non-aldol approach to
construct the polypropionate subunit from readily available mate-
rials [ 15], a highly stereoselective double hydroboration of 2,3-
allenols was developed [ 16], thus providing an alternative to the
aldol approach for accessing various stereotriads and stereotetrads
[17] in a concise manner. To demonstrate the utility of this
intriguing method, we implemented it into the total synthesis of
pironetin and described the evolution of the synthetic strategy by
adjusting the order of reaction arrays for practicability.
2. Results and discussion
To evaluate a modular strategy for future derivatization, we
envisioned the key C7 eC10 fragment bearing the four contiguous
stereogenic centers ( stereotetrad) as an essential module to be
established with the appropriate functional groups for the subse-
quent chain elongation. Accordingly, the left alkene chain and the
right pyrone motif could be readily implemented and modi ﬁed
during the synthesis that features allylation, ring-closing metath-
esis, and cross-coupling reactions. With this strategy in mind, the
synthetic plan is summarized in Scheme 1 . As an equivalent to
stereotetrad 2, the primary alcohol at C1 1 and epoxide at C6 in
intermediate 3 are therefore reserved for further conjunction. The
key intermediate epoxide 3 can be derived by a regioselective
epoxide formation and concise methylation from triol 5 which is
prepared from a stereoselective double hydroboration of 2,3-
allenol 4 [16].
Preparation of epoxide 3. The synthesis commenced with the
commercially available ( S)-Roche ester 6 (Scheme 2 ). After the
protection of the primary alcohol by a sterically bulky tert-
butyldiphenylsilyl (TBDPS) group, the corresponding methyl ester
7 was subjected to reduction with diisobutylaluminum hydride
(DIBAL-H) and was immediately applied to alkynylation with an in
situ prepared Brown propargylborane 8 [18]. The diaster-
eoselectivity of this addition was determined to be 13/1 and the
major syn-2,3-allenol 4 was obtained in a combined 62% yield after
two steps. The preparation of compound 4 was readily scaled up to
the decagram scale and the selectivity remained excellent.
Accordingly, under the optimal conditions as reported in our
previous study [ 16], the next double hydroboration was achieved
with an excellent diastereoselectivity ( ds 20/1).
Favorable syn, anti, syn-triol 5 was obtained on gram scale in 72%
yield. The subsequent formation of the terminal epoxide proved to
be challenging due to the mutual interference of the three proximal
hydroxy groups.
At the outset, the Forsyth protocol [19] was intuitively adopted
due to its generally good selectivity. The sterically bulky 2,4,6-
triisopropylphenylsulfonyl group was rationalized to react with
the primary alcohol, followed by an intramolecular SN2 substitution
via the adjacent secondary alcohol to form the requisite epoxide.
However, application to triol 5 resulted in two hard-to-separate
cyclized products in a ratio of 2/1 ( 9 and 10)( Scheme 3 a). The
mixed epoxides were subjected to the methylation and ring-
opening reaction by allylation, the isolable major diastereoisomer
was further converted into the Mosher ester 11 that was conﬁrmed
to be the desired ( R)-C7-isomer [ 20]. To our surprise, the minor
cyclized product 10 was identiﬁed as a C7-epimer of compound 9.
This unprecedented inversion during the ring-forming process is
presumably derived from the migration of the sulfonyl group from
the primary alcohol to the secondary alcohol under basic condi-
tions, thus leading to a concomitant formation of epoxide 10
(Scheme 3 b). A general survey of different sulfonyl reagents was
then undertaken to improve the yield and selectivity (entries 2 e5,
Table 1). We noticed that, with usage of other less sterically bulky
sulfonyl reagents, a considerable amount of the sulfonylated in-
termediate was accumulated and the ring-forming product was
isolated in low yields (17 e36%), indicating that the cyclization step
is a rate-determining step for such complex substance 5. Although
KHMDS can improve the overall yield of epoxides 9 and 10, the
selectivity remained unsatisfactory (entry 6 vs 1). After no signi ﬁ-
cant improvement in the yield was obtained by increasing the

equivalents of the sulfonyl reagent (data not shown) and varying
the reaction temperature (entry 7 vs 1), we turned to an approach
using the Mitsunobu reaction conditions (entries 8 and 9) [12c,21].
An adduct of phosphine with azocarboxylate is known to form a
zwitterionic intermediate that serves as a base to activate the
nucleophile. Meanwhile, the resulting ion pair also activates the
alcohol by forming a good leaving group [ 22]. To diminish the side
pathway of 5- exo-tet cyclization, external base-free conditions in
toluene with diisopropyl azodiformate (DIAD) were effective to
generate epoxides 9/10 in a combined 91% yield favoring the
desired 9 (dr 12/1) (entry 9). The reaction can be readily scaled up to
gram scale and excellent selectivity was retained. Subsequently,
methylation with methyl iodide proceeded smoothly to afford 3 in
excellent yield. A ﬁve-membered tetrahydrofuran (6% yield) was
also generated due to an involvement of the distal hydroxy group at
C9 via the 5- exo-tet cyclization pathway [ 16].
The reactivity of pyrone. With the key module 3 in hand, we
sought to introduce the C6-aldehyde moiety via a one-carbon
elongation inspired by the recent reports by Meek and others
[23,24]. Literally, a direct procedure is proposed to realize the
epoxide ring-opening by a lithiated di-[B (pin) 2]-methane reagent
and the subsequent formation of g-hydroxy bisboronate [ 23] that
can be oxidatively deboronated to form b-hydroxy aldehyde 12
(Scheme 4 a). However, this approach received no success after
several attempts by varying the reagents, reaction temperature,
and solvents. Therefore, we switched to a three-step protocol
including vinylation [ 24], silylation, and subsequent ozonolysis to
complete the requisite moiety ( Scheme 4 b).
It was interesting to ﬁnd the ﬁrst two reactions could be com-
bined without isolation of the intermediate allylic alcohol. After
subsequent ozonolysis of alkene 13, the resulting aldehyde 14,a sa
surrogate as the TBS-protected form of aldehyde 12, was subjected
to subsequent allylation. Hatakeyama and coworkers [25] extended
the Brown allylation method to the pentenylation of aldehyde in
which the Z-pentenyl diisopinocampheylborane 15 was prepared
in situ by Schlosser's method [ 26]. This tactic was also indepen-
dently developed by the Cossy group [ 27] in the total synthesis of
pironetin and other polyketides bearing such a unique pyrone
subunit [28]. The syn-allylation of aldehyde 14 was then carried out
and it was subsequently trapped by acryloyl chloride in a one-pot
procedure to deliver the acryl ester derivative of syn-stereoisomer
16 in 71% yield with a ratio of 13/1. The following RCM reaction by
the Grubbs-II catalyst [12i,29] smoothly produced pyrone 17 in 88%
isolated yield.
At this stage, we were optimistic that the planned construction
of the left chain (C12 eC14) would be straightforward. To our
surprise, treatment of pyrone 17 with tetrabutylammonium ﬂuo-
ride (TBAF) [ 30] only resulted in a dienoic acid 18 instead of
releasing the mono-desilylated compound 19 bearing a primary
alcohol at C1 1 ( Scheme 5 ). The compound 18 was apparently
formed when the allylic proton at C4 was removed under basic
conditions, via an internal ( E1cb-type) elimination way [ 31]. Acidic
conditions enforced with para-toluenesulfonic acid (TsOH) in
MeOH [12g] removed the two silyl groups to afford diol 20 and no
desired 19 was detected. The experimental result further convinced
us that this synthetic design would be a dead end when the next
oxidation only gave bislactone 21 via a facile generation of inter-
mediate lactol 20a. The challenges for the elimination and nonse-
lective silyl removal (C7/C1 1) led us to investigate the origin of
chemical selectivity through a re-evaluation of the C7-epimer 3a
(Scheme 6 ). Following the same reaction sequence, vinylation,
silylation, and ozonolysis were applied and aldehyde 23 was ob-
tained in excellent yield. Subsequent allylation and ring closing

metathesis were carried out to produce pyrone 25. Interestingly, in
the presence of TBAF, although the removal of the TBDPS group was
still unsatisfactory, the desired alcohol 26a was isolated in 37% yield
along with dienic acid 26b (20%) and caged compound 26c in 32%
yield. The latter is attributed to oxa-Michael cyclization with a free
hydroxy group at C7 while no further oxa-Michael cyclization
occurred to the diol 20, indicating the thermodynamic control for
the bicyclic tetrahydro- a-pyrone skeleton as shown in other
bioactive polyketides [32]. The slight selectivity (~2/1) favoring the
selective removal of the TBDPS group implies a possible shielding
effect due to the proximity of the pyrone ring to the OTBS group at
C7 in compound 25.
Reordering the reaction arrays. To evaluate a possible cross-
coupling tactic as proposed in the initial plan ( Scheme 1 ), we uti-
lized alcohol 26a to prepare the desired fragment ( Scheme 7 ).
However, neither Ph 3PeI2 [33] nor a two-step protocol (TsCl, trie-
thylamine, then NaI in re ﬂuxed acetone) [34] produced the desired
iodination product 27. Although tosylation occurred to yield 27a,
the subsequent cross-coupling using various transition metal-
catalyzed conditions [ 35] failed to deliver the requisite C12 eC14
vinylic motif. The low propensity toward nucleophilic substitution
of the tosylate derivative 27a may be attributed to the steric hin-
drance surrounding the reaction site, which is in sharp contrast to
the smooth transformation of the truncated structure in Cossy's
synthesis of pironetin.[ 12i]
The different reactivities of 17 and 25 toward desilylation con-
ditions provide insight into a possible conformational impact
rooted in the adjustment of the single stereogenic center. The
fragmentation of the pyrone ring suggests that the ring forming
step via the RCM reaction should be resumed at the late stage of the
synthetic sequence. Therefore, installation of the left chain was
undertaken prior to the RCM reaction for the generation of the
lactone. At this stage, Kawada's elegant solution [ 11] of introducing
the vinylic moiety via a sigmatropic rearrangement of allylic dia-
zene [36] was intriguing because the reaction site is away from the
condensed stereotetrad moiety (C7 eC10). Accordingly, compound
16 was subjected to desilylation with TBAF and the primary alcohol
28 was obtained in 86% yield (brsm) ( Scheme 8 ). Subsequent
oxidation by Dess-Martin periodinane (DMP) [ 37] and the Hor-
nereWadswortheEmmons (HWE) reaction [ 38] were performed
following a one-pot protocol to deliver the requisite E-enone 29 in
47% yield (Scheme 8). It should be noted that a severe side reaction
occurred via the Michael addition of the phosphate to the acrylate
motif at the right side of the molecule and thus the desired product
29 was then gradually consumed [ 39]. A good combined yield (80%
after two cycles) was obtained if the recovered starting material
was reintroduced into the reaction system. For the feasibility of the
current strategy toward the ﬁnal target, following Kawada's pio-
neering work, a convenient hydrazine-reduction-rearrangement
cascade was adapted to smoothly produce 31 in 85% yield. Inter-
estingly, we also applied the same reaction sequence to the 7-
epimer 26a and the complete carbon framework (i.e. 32 and 33)
was established. However, an acid removal of the TBS group of 33
resulted in several unidenti ﬁed products ( Scheme 9 ). In striking
contrast, the acidic conditions allowed the removal of the TBS
group in 31 and the target molecule was obtained ( Scheme 8). We
are delighted that the ketone reduction and desilylation could be

Evolution of a synthetic strategy . The aforementioned syn-
thetic sequence has two critical shortcomings that should be
ameliorated: (1) to diminish the undesired removal of the tert-
butyldimethylsilyl (TBS) group, delicate control of the reaction
condition must be used that may be not reproducible on a larger
scale; (2) the severe Michael addition to the acrylate group [ 39]
occurring before or after the HWE reaction reduces the isolated
yield. Consequently, the recycling of the starting materials for the
above two transformations is tedious and inef ﬁcient. Therefore, a
modiﬁcation of the synthetic strategy is urgently needed. As we
observed, the adjacent sterically demanding groups such as the
pyrone ring and acrylate group attenuate the reactivity of C7-OTBS
during the deprotection of TBDPS group at C1 1. We envisioned that
introducing an additional substituent on the acryl group, such as a
crotyl or cinnamyl group, may be helpful for shielding the C7-
silyloxy group under the desilylation conditions, and more impor-
tantly, the extent of the Michael addition reaction to the
a,b-un-
saturated ester can be diminished due to the steric hindrance at the
b-position.
Accordingly, the homoallylic alcohol derived from the allylation
of aldehyde 14 was immediately quenched by esteri ﬁcation with
crotonoyl chloride and cinnamoyl chloride, respectively. However,
crotonoylation proved to be inappropriate due to the migration of
the double bond (i.e., 34) in the presence of an organic base [ 40]
(Scheme 10 ). A preliminary screening of different bases such as
triethylamine and diisopropylethylamine did not ef ﬁciently pre-
vent such an isomerization. On the other hand, in the presence of
triethylamine, cinnamate 35 was obtained in good overall yield
(78%).
To our delight, the next desilylation indeed proceeded well and
the primary alcohol 36 was obtained in 82% yield without an
appreciable amount of diol (such as a compound like 20 in Scheme
5) contamination. The subsequent oxidation and HWE reaction
were carried out smoothly at an elevated temperature (45 /C14 C) and
E-enone 37 was obtained in 78% isolated yield without the denoted
impurity derived from Michael addition. Although the completion
of the RCM reaction required an elevated temperature (100 /C14 C) in
toluene, the resulting enone-pyrone 30 was obtained in a good
isolated yield (80%). Repeating the established one-pot protocol
including the enone reduction and desilylation with HCl completed
the synthesis of pironetin ( 1).
3. Conclusion
In summary, we discussed here the evolution of a synthetic
strategy toward pironetin by changing the order of the reaction
arrays based on the dead ends and inef ﬁciency encountered in the
synthetic efforts [ 41]. Several notable features can be drawn from
here: (1) the facile fragmentation of the pyrone ring should be
taken into consideration in future synthesis because this structural
motif is embedded in several bioactive polyketides; (2) the use of
the acryl group that commonly used for the construction of the
pyrone ring via an RCM reaction involves a Michael addition when a
soft nucleophile is applied and the cinnamyl group is suggested to
be utilized as a surrogate; (3) a conformational change derived
from the one-site switch of the chiral centers is also crucial for an
array of the subsequent chemical transformations. These ﬁndings
are clearly valuable for devising an ef ﬁcient synthesis for complex
polyketides with the criteria of practicability [ 42], even for a target
molecule as small as pironetin. Guided by the versatility of the
stereotetrad-centered strategy, application in the construction of
more complex bioactive polyketides is currently underway in this
laboratory and will be reported in due course.
